questions.title: Call the chosen pricing strategy
questions.prompt: checkout receives a base price and a pricing function. Call that function exactly once with the base price and return its result. Inputs stay in int range. The caller chooses the policy.
questions.signature: int checkout(int base, const std::function<int(int)>& policy)

tests.label: Fixed discount
tests.hint: Use the supplied policy instead of hard-coding a price.

tests.label: Different policy
tests.hint: The same checkout function must support another policy.

tests.label: Free policy
tests.hint: Zero is a legitimate policy result.

tests.label: Exactly one call
tests.hint: Calling a policy twice can repeat its side effects.

hints: The policy is callable with one integer argument.
Strategy separates the choice of a rule from the code that uses it.
questions.explanation: The caller supplies behavior. A callable is enough for this small variation point; a class hierarchy is useful only when the policy needs a richer interface.

questions.title: Wrap a renderer with brackets
questions.prompt: Keep the Renderer alias. bracket(next) returns a new renderer that calls next once and surrounds its result with [ and ]. Store the wrapped callable by value so the returned callable stays valid. Nested wrappers must compose.
questions.driver: int main(){std::string s;std::getline(std::cin,s);auto render=bracket([](std::string text){return text;});std::cout<<render(s)<<"\n";}

tests.label: One wrapper
tests.hint: Wrap the returned text, not the original input only.

tests.label: Preserve inner behavior
tests.hint: Call the wrapped renderer before adding brackets.

tests.label: Empty text
tests.hint: Empty output still gets its wrapper.

hints: Return a lambda that captures next by value.
Capturing the local parameter by reference would dangle after bracket returns.
questions.explanation: Each wrapper keeps the same calling interface and adds one behavior around the next component. Value capture preserves the wrapped callable’s lifetime.

questions.title: Publish to a stable listener snapshot
questions.prompt: Complete Signal::publish. Call subscribers in registration order. Subscribers added during a publication must start receiving events only on the next publication. No unsubscribe or concurrent access is required.
questions.signature: class Signal: void subscribe(std::function<void(int)>); void publish(int)

tests.label: Registration order
tests.hint: Visit the snapshot in its stored order.

tests.label: Value delivered
tests.hint: Pass the published value to the listener.

tests.label: New listener waits
tests.hint: Iterate over a snapshot, not the vector being changed.

tests.label: No listeners
tests.hint: An empty subscriber list is valid.

hints: Adding to the original vector while iterating it may invalidate iteration.
Copy the listener list before invoking callbacks.
questions.explanation: The snapshot makes the notification boundary explicit and avoids iterator invalidation caused by new subscribers. It does not make the signal thread-safe or define recursive publication policies.
